Don't be discouraged by the negative reviews, the game is great and worth trying out.  As a sequel to Spire 1, it's mechanically the same, but with much more interesting boss rewards (ancient boons) and an alternative Act 1. I expect alternative Acts 2 and 3 to greatly increase not just variety but also strategic depth because you will have to prepare for twice as many challenges while drafting in Act 1. There are two new characters, and all of the characters ported from Spire 1 have new synergy spaces. Status Defect is peak. If you are new to Spire, it's important to realize that Spire is a game that leans hardcore; the base difficulty, A0, is meant to be challenging for people new to Spire, while the highest difficulty, A10, is meant to be challenging even for people who have spent hundreds of hours playing. Do not feel like you have to play on higher difficulty just because it exists. You may face challenges that feel insurmountable, but one of most fun aspects of playing Spire is dying to some elite or boss, recognizing that you might want to be wary of that enemy, drafting cards strong against that enemy in future runs, and improving at the game in the process.

I was genuinely excited for Slay the Spire 2 because the first game is one of the best roguelike deckbuilders ever made. The gameplay foundation is still strong, but finding out that Anita Sarkeesian was brought in as a consultant honestly raised some concerns for me.  Whether people agree with her or not, she has been a very divisive figure in gaming for years, and for many players her involvement is seen as a red flag because it often signals unnecessary ideological influence being brought into games instead of focusing purely on gameplay and player experience.  What frustrates me most is that developers keep involving controversial consultants without being transparent about what their role actually was. Maybe her involvement was minor, maybe not — but when players see names associated with activism and culture-war discussions attached to a beloved franchise, it naturally creates distrust.  I play games to escape politics and modern social messaging, not to wonder whether creative decisions were filtered through consultants pushing a particular worldview. Even if the gameplay is still solid, this kind of decision hurts my confidence in the future direction of the franchise.  I’m not leaving this review out of hate. I just think developers should understand that many longtime gamers are tired of ideological influence creeping into entertainment, especially in franchises that never needed it in the first place.

I have played cards games for over two decades and accumalted thousands of hours total in rogulites like Slay the Spire I, Monster Train, Monster Train II, Across the Obelisk, Vault of the Void, Indies Lies and I have reached top ranks at multiplayer card games such as Hearthstone and Shadowverse. My takeaway from all those games is simple:   There's a fine line between well designed difficulty and overreliance on RNG that leaves you hanging dry unless you're offered the right options at the right time. Slay the Spire II suffers from low value upgrades, (slightly) overtuned enemy damage, and partially overtuned oppressive boss mechanics. It does get better once you have more versatile cards unlocked and it is doable if you find the right relics at the right time; but overall - looking at all the card game rogulites I played in the past - Slay the Spire II falls among those where I felt that my decision making had the least impact on the outcome of the run; or in other words - balance is still lacking severely, resulting in a huge performance difference based on RNG.  As much as I want to like Slay the Spire II because of nostalgia for Slay the Spire I, currently it definitely ranks amongst the worse rogulike card games. Should Early-Access improve, I will update this review, but for now I am simply disappointed.

Pros:  - Fun gameplay loop - Interesting card mechanics - Co-op play - Visuals and Audio are good - Decent enemy variety  It's enjoyable, especially if you are playing with friends. Even some mechanics like Sly from Silent or Summon from Necrobinder are interesting, which can lead to fun decks to build. For the team that has spawned a genre, I am glad that they released a sequel that is enjoyable, even amongst my friends that don't usually play card games. We've played until we finished Ascension 10 a few times since that is the current end game limit and are waiting for more updates to come.  Cons: - Balancing seems more focused making cards in line with other cards, viable but not fun, more nerfs over buffing - No gameplay resume on co-op - Hiring someone that has a record of bad faith behaviour/attitude towards games  If you are aware of Arrowhead's approach to Helldivers 2 balancing in it's first few months, then you basically know that this is the same pattern. Rather than trying to improve cards more, they only increase maybe a few but nerf a lot. I understand that there are stupid decks (like ones that let you infinitely stack on a single turn) but they are more looking to make things less fun and more of a struggle. All decks can work normally but once you introduce ascension, they make you focus on certain builds that can be fun but just ensure they aren't getting screwed over. You should prioritise what makes decks fun to play but also other decks that could be viable and fun if the cost/benefits were there.   Multiplayer is also rough because if someone has a bad connection, the game needs to reset into the lobby and play again from the start of the battle.  Then, the team hiring Anita Sarkeesian was really a bad PR move and also, when time will tell, the direction of the game will be worse off. For those who don't know, she is one of the original people that caused 'Gamergate' back in 2014. Since then she's actively attacked gamers for liking their own industry for what makes things fun and pushes agendas to fit their 'unrealistic' idealogies. Games are meant to be an escape, a medium where you can just enjoy yourself and take a break from reality. With the unfortunate shift of Western developers looking to make you want to believe and play a certain way, other companies have given a lot more agency to players to decide how they engage in their games providing the tools related to the game.   Conclusion: I am giving a benefit of the doubt that because it's Early Access, there is a lot of fine tuning to be done. As of now, I can't really recommend the game in it's current state. Right now it's a 'depends on if you want to try it out' but since there is no neutral review, because of more negatives outweighing the benefits, I cannot recommend it. It's fun the first few gameplays but the direction that it's going towards is not something I can confidently ask others to partake in.

Mega Crit had something rare: a game respected almost entirely for its mechanics, replayability, balance, and design. Dragging that into political and ideological baggage is reckless, arrogant, and unnecessary.  This is not what I supported. This is not what many long-time players wanted. If Mega Crit wants the trust of its audience, it should be transparent about why this consultant was involved, what influence she had, and why the studio thought this was acceptable. The thing that has thrown me off is that at time of writing I find the game HARD. In StS1 I could reasonably expect to make it to Act 2 or 3s final boss pretty regularly, even if I made a mistake or two along the way. I pretty regularly have trouble making it past the boss of the first Act, and in some cases past the ELITEs of the first act in StS2. Thank you in advance, I am aware I should git gudd.  My personal theory/feeling is that this is due to how encounters work in StS2.  In StS1 I felt like most enemy encounters were relatively static: they presented a relatively fixed threat level. If you could block for "x" you could mitigate most of the threat, and eventually take them down without taking too much damage. This wasn't always the case, notably the cultists using Ritual, some(most?) elites and obviously the bosses,  but most encounters didn't feel like they scaled inside of the encounter itself.  In StS2 enemies that don't have a way to give themselves permanent boosts to strength are, I believe, at least less common than enemies that can't. I want to say "enemies that can't buff themselves are the [i]exception[/i]" but I don't want to risk being hyperbolic. This means most encounters are a race not to beat a relatively consistent threat, but against snowballs that will inevitably outscale anything you can reasonably handle outside of infinite or meme builds.  My lightbulb moment was fighting the Sewer Clam, which on Turn 7 was swinging at me with +12 strength. It was the fourth encounter on Act 1, a regular enemy room. After digging further into it the wiki suggests that the claim gives itself +4 strength every other turn, which matches my experience. What throws me for a loop is comparing this against Donu and Deca, Act 3 bosses from StS1. Donu [i]also[/i] buffs himself (and Deca), permanent increasing their strength every other turn. By [i]3[/i]. A random mook on the first act of the second game has a stronger permanent self-buff than a boss of Act 3 of the first game. I am aware of the fact that the extra damage is scarier on Donu/Deca because they each hit twice, it's still wild to me, and acts as a great microcosm of my experience with lot of the game's encounter design.  So yeah, game is polished already, in EA so I expect balance will get there, and I've gotten my money's worth, so it gets a thumbs up, but I'd probably have enjoyed it more as a full release and EA has kinda put me off of it. I might finish my timeline as it exists for "completion" but I probably won't revisit it on full release.

I already have more hours in this than the first game, so figure it out yourself (and I think first one is a masterpiece). I love it! A few points to mention, though.  Balance here is all over the place. Clone is OP, quite a few interactions between relics and cards are OP (some easier to get than others). It's expected since it's just an Early Access. I'm not complaining though - difficulty wise I can tell that A10 in this game is comparable to A20 in StS1, but not as grindy to get to, which is really nice. Balance between characters is non-existent. I can win 30 to 40 percent of Clad runs on A10, but for the love of God I cannot win a single run with Regent. Regent is my favorite character btw, so I have most runs on them. But they're difficult to win with, at least on the highest ascention. Animations and visuals overall are a glow up from the first game. When I first saw this, I was not sure if I like it or not visually. But now, when I watch old content from Spire 1, I doubt I had eyes at that point in time. Fonts, card arts, enemy animations and sprites are SUPERB. I love how it feels to play.  Audio in this game is good. Music is a solid successor to the first game, nothing to complain about. Love that some enemies already have their unique sounds.  And what about mechanics?  If you played the first game, you know that there are boss relics. A unique set of relics that offer much stronger, one off benefits, often including additional energy every turn, with a significant downside. This game has an alternative, and what an alternative it is! Ancients are NPCs that welcome you after each act to offer strong upgrades to your run, with much (MUCH) more difersity than classic boss relics from the first game. Even Neow got their upgrades sorted out, and a few more getting added with patches on a Beta branch. Overall this is the strongest upgrade for me. Enemies? I feel the change to recognizable patterns in enemy intents is a welcome change. Enemies overall feel more difficult, but the fact that you can predict what they can do on their next turn is cool. Augments on cards feel interesting, but I'm not a big fan of Queens Bound augment that allows you to play only 1 card out of 3 possible. When it comes to the Doormaker, that developers already removed on the Beta branch, I have a strong opinion that this decision was a bit rushed because of how some players just didn't figure this fight out. It felt like a third act boss more than any other. It didn't counter any build as many say, as you could potentially win with a smaller deck or draw heavy deck. And yes, I've beat his ass with souls build on Necromancer on A10, so skill issue, I guess. Also, nerf Decimillipede, it killed more of my runs than any other enemy in the game.  Characters?  3 out of 4 classic characters return in this game, with familiar mechanics, but with an addition of new ones too. Ironclad got some cool cards that expand his strength and exhaust synergies, Silent got a new keyword (that existed in the first game as a mechanic but didn't have a name), and Defect got completely new archetype with status cards (awesome, you should try it out!). For the new characters, I think Regent is the highlight, offering not only quite a few brand new card mechanics, but a completely new concept - a separate energy source that doesn't exhaust at the end of the turn. Necromancer is an honorable mention, I love interactions with Osty, soul builds and Doom mechanic, but it felt more one sided at the moment. Overall: I just love how the developers mix those mechanics, offering Sly cards that interact with Shivs, Status cards that interact with Orbs, and Forge cards that would love you to gain more stars. This is what it's all about - not fall into a single archetype, but build unique solutions for every fight that you have to face, prepared in advance, because the end goal always is to Slay the Spire! 9 out of 10 at the moment of this review. Changes like that make the game more interesting, since, if you start a Silent run, you can't assume you're going to see at least one Acrobatics by the end of the second Act.  However, the Dev team has also been receptive to criticism. When a similarly strong Silent card, Preparation, was totally redesigned - the player base loudly complained and the change was rolled back to preserve the flavor and identity of the class. Altogether I think the Dev team has shown a lot of maturity in how they handle designing a sequel to their cult classic game, which, I must stress, isn't even out yet. If you like a deckbuilding roguelike, STS2 is a great option.  Also, a lot of the people review bombing the first time have no conception of how often STS1 changed after its release. Slay the Spire 2 is a phenomenal game. It has everything I want in a roguelike: challenging gameplay, thoughtful card design, and downright addictive replay value.  Since it is still in Early Access, I definitely would not say it is perfect in every regard. But honestly, that is also where STS2 stands out above a lot of other games. The development team has been exceptionally communicative, responsive to feedback, and genuinely seems committed to making the best version of this game possible. It is beyond refreshing to see a game that feels like it is being made for the players, not just built to squeeze out as much money as possible.  I have clearly put a lot of time into this game, and I will continue to do so. The first Slay the Spire quite literally saved my life. I will not go into detail on that, but I am beyond grateful for this series and for the developers behind it. I fully believe in this game and its continued development.  That being said, my biggest complaint is not even really with the game. It is with the community.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the community can be downright infuriating. From review bombing to childish tantrums over changes that have not even fully played out yet, watching parts of the community try to bully their way into getting what they want is frustrating. As gamers, we constantly complain about triple-A games being overpriced, unfinished, soulless, and built around monetization instead of fun. STS2 is the opposite of that. We have a responsive development team, a game that is already well worth its price, and a satisfying foundation that is actively being improved.  And the response from some people is to throw childlike tantrums on the internet?  You can literally send feedback directly to the team through the game. You can be passionate, critical, and invested in wanting the game to improve without trying to damage its reputation in the process. Supporting a team like this should be a no-brainer. Acting otherwise just helps justify the exact kind of gaming industry people claim to hate. Enjoy Call of Duty 30 for the low price of $199.99, I guess.  My only real complaint is that parts of the gaming community have become exhausting to watch. I hope the team keeps creating, experimenting, and perfecting Slay the Spire 2. This game deserves patience, support, and honest feedback — not tantrums.  Highly recommended.

STS2 right now is built like one of those modpacks you might come across in well loved games that are designed by and for people with thousands of hours poured into the vanilla experience where the learning curve and basic balance are not even tertiary concerns in the face of just making the game more challenging when everything else has been memorized and optimized. The problem is that STS2 is being sold as a full product and can reasonably be expected to be people's first experience with that kind of game, in which case it's incredibly frustrating.  Runs in STS2 either take off at orbital velocities and become unstoppable or they die sad, pathetic deaths against a considerably harsher roster of encounters. It's not uncommon for your average hallway fight to be harder than some of STS1's nastiest elites. Most of the "easier" cards to build around are now gone and replaced no real equivalence, which further destroys accessibility for newcomers. Ascension climbs much more rapidly, but the base A0 entry point is also harder by an order of magnitude.  There's obviously a lot of buzz about this game but I think it's quite telling that a crushing majority of the positive opinions about this game come from people who have absolutely polished the first game clean. Roguelites have this kind of problem sometimes where they have to contend with a sequel being both "the first game but harder" but also potentially the entry point for many people, which is why STS2 isn't just throwing everything out but obviously is trying at its core to revamp and overhaul aspects of the first game.  I kind of found my experience with STS2 unpleasant. I very quickly lost the drive to keep my patience through profoundly uninteresting runs. More than frustration, what I felt playing it after a while was ennui. I really hope this game eventually manages to be built around having an actual learning curve that does not involve either hundreds of hours of unmitigated pain and frustration or looking up optimal builds to aim for to optimize the fun out of the learning experience. If you're the kind of guy to already have four digit playtime in the first game you can safely ignore this review and get in, but I wouldn't recommend this thing for newcomers. It's a terrible first impression for anyone who might have heard good things about Slay the Spire.

This review is subject to change should gameplay quality improve.  Coming from being a lover of the previous game, and wanting to play STS with friends, the sequel has provided at least that much. Alongside new characters, reworks to the original ones, and new challenges in the climb, it does accomplish a sequel's goal of building off of its predecessor well.  Now for why this is a negative review.  To begin, why on God's good Earth would a company with a cult following and almost certain success with a sequel to a beloved game sign on a consultant who has made her fame over the past decade for attacking and harassing gamers, the gaming community as a whole, and anyone who dares not share her aggressive ideology? Were you held hostage, Megacrit? Was this some sort of tithe given as payment for some sort of blackmail? What was the expectation of benefit for the game and your business to have a radioactive person like her onboard? Thankfully, the gameplay doesn't seem too deeply affected by this inclusion, but these people cannot be seriously considered anything more than enemies of the gaming community as a whole, to pay one as a consultant has been the mark of death for a dozen games before.  Now for less current event issues: The game feels much more difficult than the previous game, but not for the same reasons. When I failed a run in STS1, I had misplayed or run out of options and didn't have the health to soak the consequences. In STS2, you can just die at any point because a non-elite enemy chip-damaged your max HP to 0, a non-elite enemy had an opening gambit of a 12+ dmg attack and a buff, or the actual ELITE enemies apply max-stacks of crippling debuffs onto you in a single turn and obliterate you for taking too long. By turn 4. The difficulty doesn't feel fair, like you can make a variety of builds work. It feels like the game is tuned for an insane meta that some characters keep pace with better than others, but that just isn't fulfilling. It doesn't feel fair in that when you fail, you don't feel like there was anything you could even do to salvage the situation or do differently, you just failed to scale as insanely fast as the game arbitrarily decided you should have. That alongside nearly every single enemy in the game being able to strength boost infinitely makes the idea of a defensive build impossible to take seriously anymore. Enemies will always hit you harder next turn than they did last turn, in one way or another. And if they didn't, it's because they gained ~4-7 strength stacks instead to blast through you next turn. That's not fun gameplay, that's a stat-check.  Multiplayer is particularly punishing in that regard. Enemy health is at least doubled PER PLAYER, which wouldn't be as bad if damage wasn't ALSO spiked to the moon in a similar way. Many of our multiplayer runs start by getting whacked by double digit damage through our block on the opening turns. With 14 floors left to go before we can get to Act 2. The upside to multiplayer is that if one player gets lucky (or necrobinders hard enough), they can carry the entire team by managing to match the scaling. Anyone who doesn't get lucky or make a god build ends up becoming dead weight and just pumping the stats on the enemies, causing more difficult encounters for the people who actually can participate in them. I've been on both sides of this extreme multiple times, and it's not a good sign of game design for there to not be a flow state of difficulty and challenge to recovery and growth for the next challenge. This isn't so much as a diffculty curve as much as it is an exponential chart where the equation skips a few X values every 5 units.  If you want to play STS multiplayer, I'd suggest Together In Spire, it's very well made and has multiple characters and converted bosses with their own unique decks, really a labor of love to the game. If you want to try out being a lazy star king and a cursed skeleton, consider picking up this game. If you liked the original and want to support the devs, consider picking up this game but more preferably share the original around with friends. If you want to experience more slay the spire content and this game is looking to provide just that, I recommend browsing the workshop for STS1 instead.  For the time being, a message needs to be sent that a player vs developer mentality is caustic for game design and that no community should bear for it's creatives to be advised by its enemies.  It's got my money, but make your own decision.

Beautiful game.   Loved the extended lore, the artwork, the immersive events. Loved the new characters! StS 1 mostly gave you more energy as boss drops - here, there's diverse options that challenge you to really think about the strengths and weaknesses of your deck and how you want to develop it - but that turn out as strong, or stronger, than just being able to spend more each turn.  The muliplayer mode is an incredible boost, with dedicated cards that work for the entire group, or support other players. The only small drawback to this so far is the Ironclad's weakness of almost never getting enough block (carried over from StS 1). This resulted in us going through some intensely frustrating runs where Ironclad got the rare Tank power early without ever getting more than two or three block cards over the entire run - or constantly getting offered cards working with said inexistent block (Body Slam!). We still love multiplayer, hanging out with friends or partners, giving each other boosts, and finding out about the synergies of the different characters.  re Difficulty: I made it to Ascension 10 with two characters pretty fast, one of them Necrobinder (new). This honestly surprised me, given that my highest on StS 1 was still 15/20, after years of playing. I still would not consider StS 2 as lacking challenge. I find it a little unfortunate that the game is suffering from its own success, having drawn a large enough crowd to include people that don't seem to understand what the game is doing. It's fine to want to win at a game playing your way and not having to think too hard, and there are plenty of games that let you do that. But this game isn't (and can't be) for everyone. I feel bad for anyone who hoped to figure out a simple, reproducible strategy and then win every time while choosing the same cards, but that honestly sounds like a garbage game to me. I don't want to play a deckbuilding roguelike where I build the same deck each time.  I put 1500+ hours into StS1 and I've already put several hundred into this one because they have the depth to not only allow but demand that each run be played differently. This is challenging but rewarding, each run feels like a new puzzle. I want to be challenged and have to think on my toes and adapt when the card I want doesn't show up in a card reward or my draws really suck for a whole fight so I need to plan a new route through the act. And thankfully it seems like that's what the devs are trying to make. It's unfortunate that some people didn't get that and got drawn into a popular game that wasn't their cup of tea. But if learning a challenging game where success relies on your wit every time sounds fun to you, then I can't recommend this game enough.

Those who were already happy with StS1 have new features to look into (new characters, multiplayer, new cards, etc.), but may find that the changes are too subtle.  What is this game? It's a roguelike deckbuilder, which means you have a deck of cards that you improve over the course of a playthrough, and that every playthrough is theoretically unique since it is procedurally generated using a "seed".  Why is it good? There is a bit of a challenge and learning curve to this game, though it's significantly reduced if you have played games like Hearthstone or Magic: the Gathering. The appeal tends to lie in the challenge, and the satisfying feeling that arises when a highly synergetic deck comes together. The animations and art also show marked improvements from the original game.  Anecdote: I tried the board game version of this with a couple family members. For starters, I got this after the recent review-bombing, and I'd like to say, I honestly don't understand why people are complaining. I looked at reviews prior to purchasing and noticed a lot of people were complaining about balancing changes made to the Doormaker that made Act 3 almost impossible to beat if you got him as the boss, and as far as I know, these changes were only made to the beta branch of the game testing. I've fought this boss a couple of times, and while challenging, I've never found it to be unfair, and it punishing infinite decks is actually good for the game imo. Infinite decks were broken in STS I (i.e. Defect w/Claw + Unceasing Top), with the only counter being the Spire heart (a completely optional boss in order to unlock ascensions). Both of these games are challenging, and I appreciate Mega Crit attempting to increase the challenge in a way that feels natural while still feeling fair. Plus, once again, them balancing infinite decks to be less broken helps to shake up playstyles so the game doesn't feel as monotonous using one kind of deck every run because it's practically an instant win. Overall, pretty much the same gameplay loop as STS I, with some new interesting characters that really change up the way you play. The art and animation is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stunning too, overall just an amazing refinement of what they had in the first game. Obviously, it's still in Early Access, so content may be lacking in some places, but I've been playing for nearly 20 hours and I don't see myself running out of things to do anytime soon. Lastly, let's not forget one of the biggest additions to this game from the first; the multiplayer. I genuinely didn't know how they'd adapt the gameplay to work for Multiplayer Co-Op, but it works very well here. Allowing up to four players to do a run together with the 5 different characters (as of writing this review) really shakes up gameplay with unique cards and events to multiplayer runs along with the countless potential synergies between you and your friends, adding a whole new layer to builds by essentially allowing three different character builds to coalesce and make one big party deck build. STS II has been a wonderful experience so far with Co-Op and Singleplayer, and I'm looking forward to how the game will look as we get closer toward its full release.

Slay the Spire 2 has been an excellent return to the classic Slay the Spire (StS1) gameplay, with the inclusion of cooperative gameplay which is something desperately missing from modern game development, with the prevalence of AI slop and underdeveloped titles relying on PvP mechanics.  The game hasn’t been without controversy owing to recent patches, and commitment to a challenging experience – where not every run of the game presents you the opportunity of victory. Much like games such as FTL or Peglin, loss makes up part of the gameplay and the journey to the loss is part of the enjoyment. Likewise to those games meta progression is very minor, and only offers new ways to play the game rather than direct improvement, so it is up to the player to make good choices for the highest likelihood of success.  In game development, this struggle against sometimes impossible, or nearly impossible odds is usually referred to as Hard fun as oppose to Casual, Creative or Narrative fun, and balancing patches have moved the game towards these harder struggles causing the controversy.  However; It’s just a different kind of gameplay, not one that was falsely advertised or unexpected. One that a lot of us find more enjoyable (dozens of us!). I relish the patches preventing infinite looping builds, because they become boring quickly – especially in a multiplayer setting, watching a friend deal 2 damage every three looped cards to kill a boss. Sure victories are fewer and sometimes rarely possible, but are savored.  I find the negative review bombing, and salinity towards the gameplay poor faith. The game is good quality by near every metric; replayable, cheap, large and diverse content.  It’s just less casual. Treasured time more than a cheap win. So save your negative review for a developer actually screwing you over.

EDIT for Constructive Feedback: The game is heavily reliant on RNG right now (despite what the fans may say). However, I think there are ways to balance that which will make the game positively different from the first one, while also making reasonable sense from a Role-Play perspective and retaining the core loop. To balance RNG, the solution is expanding player choice and options. I think there are 2 core ways in which this can be implemented, plus a bonus 1:    First, give the players a choice before each act to choose which region they would like to travel to (it would make sense that our characters are not braindead idiots that only know how to walk forward). This can increase agency over the run, and allows the devs to implement some additional agency tools, such as the region choice screen telling us what kind of card rewards are more likely in said region. (For example, this can be a small RNG tweek to card family spawn rate. When you are playing as the Ironclad, path A gives more Exhaust cards, path B gives more Self Damage cards, and this is randomized).    SECOND, give the option for players to reroll shop cards for a fee, and perhaps to see useless relics. The logical sense of selling relics is obvious, there is no reason for your character to be carrying useless trinkets on him during his tiresome journey. The pay to reroll once is just a basic mechanic for a lot of roguelikes, which increases agency.   As a bonus, I think it would make sense for us to get to customize the starting deck a bit and give a few relic choices for each charact, so each character feels more different. At this point, I think the 5 strike, 5 defend standard is just bad design, because these cards are wayyy underpowered. We could have some options with tradeoffs, such as Necrobinder actually being able to start with a Doom or such card, which then we can remove if that is not the build you want. Makes no sense for a freaking King to be entering the tower with the same basic stuff as a nomad, for example.    Point being: MORE PLAYER AGENCY = MORE FUN.  ORIGINAL REVIEW: I think this game suffers from the same problem that StS1 does, and on a greater scale: RNGesus reliance. Addressing the comments ahead of time: This is not a matter of "get good", its a matter of balancing the game in a way that the players are not reliant on RNG and restarts.   When you first start the game, it is somewhat easier to make a solid build because the reward pool is smaller and balanced around making it viable to beat the game. However, as you unlock more cards and relics, your odds of getting the rewards you need for the build you want to make go down down down. This makes it so that the game feels charming at the beginning, but unrewarding as you progress.    I have played some of StS 1, and honestly, it just feels like a masochistic passtime most of the time. When you get lucky its great, but when you don't you also don't get any opportunities to recover. This made me drop the 1st game, and only play the 2nd on CoOp, which suffers from the same problem, but this time with company.    In both games, you can get a great rare card at the start, and then spent the rest of act 1 and 2 without getting anything to make the build you want. This makes the game a test of endurance and luck, instead of skill. Most times I die is the enemy attacking for 30 or more three times in a row, which gives me no time to do anything else.    As some people pointed out, I do agree that the lack of energy relics makes the game less fun than the 1st, because enemies can often do multiple moves in the same turn among attack, buff, debuff, summon minions, or shield, while you need to use your entire turn to stop even one of those actions.    Point is, I would not play this game if it wasn't for my friends. Misery loves company though, so the game can be kinda fun when it goes well.

Look, I WANT the game to be good. I've played a lot of the game too; and I will continue to play it long after this review. Why do I not recommend it then, right? To answer this more effectively, I'll divide my review between 1-2 players and 3-4 players because I feel vastly different between them  3-4 players: I feel this is where the game starts to shine, the multiplayer cards and the interactions between classes/characters can create unique and fun runs that leave you wanting to recreate the same thrill on another run. The game is genuinely easier with more players, but that isn't why I give it a good rating. Having more players can allow you to win vs a monster/boss that is a hard counter which completely flattens a deck without much counter play.  I also do love how each character genuinely plays unique to any other character in the game. It doesn't become "ironclad but shaped like a skeleton" because each set of cards has their own unique style of cards that push the player to a different playstyle and it is fun to play in the different ways.   ================================================== 1-2 players:  If I have such a positive reaction to 3-4 players, why do I feel that a negative review is in order?  Balance.  It is the single most frustrating thing about this game; nothing else even comes close. The game is just simply not balanced in a way that makes single and duo player of this game even remotely fun when you stop and think about your loss. I have beaten this game countless times when playing with 3 and 4 players. But don't get me wrong, I've lost so much more than I have won even on 3 and 4 players, but the number of times I have won on single player? 3. Exactly 3 times (as of this review). Duo is similar in terms of victories.   I understand that you cannot block all damage or nuke an enemy down before they can get their chance to hurt you; I'm not advocating for the game to be easy. I LIKE the challenge that the game has, sometime forcing you to chose between two bad options. But my major issue comes from bad balance through overtuned enemies or bosses that Hard Counter decks and playstyles. Elites like Entomancer or Decimillipede can completely bulldoze a multi hit deck with the deck having very poor or no capacity of counter play because they're built to completely shut down a playstyle.  A slow whittle down and eventual loss doesn't feel bad, it makes me want to improve my choices and do better the next run, but the majority of run ending encounters see me wiped out from 50%-100% HP to dead because I cannot fight the enemy as they are a hard counter to the deck I am playing.  Bad hands/bad deck draws are RNG, you cannot be mad or upset that you just simply got bad RNGesus luck, that's just RNG. But so many of the enemies are overtuned to the point where drawing great hand in your deck will still result in you taking lots of damage that will ultimately end your run when you're unlucky enough to draw a bad hand. When you're completely screwed on adding cards you needed to your deck because the game refused to give you a single block card, it sucks but that is the nature of RNG games like Slay the Spire.  I will reiterate, I WANT this game to be good but the game devs are taking the approach that Helldivers took at the start of that game. Just applying nerfs to anything that does well instead of addressing the enemies that feel a bit overtuned and impossible to fight in single and duo player without getting lucky with the right cards. Reached my 100 hours mark and want to share my current experience with the game. I basically only play two player coop with my buddy, and finished A10 two player coop in the latest beta-branch. The high ascension coop experience feels like the end of a journey that dragged itself too long.  Let us start with things I do enjoy:  1. very nice art that is constantly improving, I also like the funny beta art, hopefully they can be accessed at the official launch. 2. Interesting enemy design, each enemy feels different and requires different tool kits to solve. The current door maker is more unique than the first edition and I am all for design that is unique and interesting. 3. Relatively smooth coop experience, haven't experience a lot of crashes or bugs during coop.  Now on to the negatives: 1. Lack of coop element: though there are a lot of coop cards, they are usually hidden under the colorless card poll. There have been runs neither of us picked up any coop cards. I hope they add more class-specific coop cards and events that provides coop cards. 2. Lack of coop interactions: the coop cards and statuses are basically all there is to it in coop, and most coop cards are straight up just provide defence or damage and lack meaningful and interest interactions. 3. Deck building under high ascension is very limited: there are only 3 bosses in act 3, and we need to fight 2 of them in a10. In two player coop those bosses are very difficult and require very different solve, making the end deck very similar. 4. Lack of player expression in game play for high ascension: because the monsters hp are very high in coop, it is very unlikely to pursue strategies that kills enemy quickly. So even in hallway fights the game play is just weak the enemy and use power, which feels really repetitive. Adding the fact that the end deck require solves for the final boss, not only is the deck similar between runs, the fights are similar within runs.  These are my current thoughts on specifically two player coop. At the current stage it definitely needs some polishing, hopefully it will get more fun and more interactive.

Slay the Spire 2. It's Slay the Spire, but 2.  The first game singlehandedly founded a genre and then remained as its king for something around seven years. This one is poised to inherit the throne. In its current state it's already one of the best deckbuilders around, with fairly simple card and relic effects applied against fairly simple yet well designed (aesthetically and mechanically) enemies leading nevertheless to immense levels of tactics, and it's not even remotely finished (tho in terms of bugs or other problems this early access indie is in a better state than plenty of finished AAA games). The idea of alternate acts to break up the monotony (act 1 for now, act 2 and 3 later) is a welcome addition, the ancient boons are a much better way of handling end of act rewards than the old boss chest (but shoutout to darv for still bringing those boss relics to sts 2) and while it would've been neat to give the watcher another try and have her be properly balanced i'm way happier to see these two new guys because they're really fun to play (iirc they're planning on adding even more, plus the act 4).  As for the white beast statue in the room, as mentioned the game is in early access. This means that the balancing of things, while pretty good, is not yet as tight as sts 1, and specifically it's still bound to change a lot until release with cards being nerfed and buffed and reworked and removed. It's not as bad as it sounds, if anything i find it fun to have the meta shaken up every week or two hence why i play the beta branch, but a wide portion of the playerbase heavily disagrees to the point of reviewbombing the game into a mixed (maybe even negative, haven't checked if it changed) score that it absolutely doesn't deserve. Please ignore these crybabies, they are just mad because the balance is being skewed towards actually playing the game and interacting with its systems as opposed to finding a broken infinite combo and using that for every fight on every run, and instead of using the *in-game feedback button* to voice their concerns they reviewbomb the early access game for not having a definitive balance yet. A lot of the negative reviews are players upset about infinites being nerfed, and the design decisions (in the early access BTW) gearing towards making infinites harder to make work. I personally think this is a great direction for the game. Infinites are funny and all every so often, but if you are able to consistently get infinites going nearly every run, what is the point? This game is a roguelike deckbuilder. I want to be able to adapt my deck to the challenges put before me not guide a build toward the same archetype every run. Every run should not feel similar or the same due to infinites being even a little bit consistent. This is why the watcher was the least fun character in the first StS in my opinion. Why do any other fun build when you are consistently going to get shut down way more and think "why didn't I just do a rushdown build".   A lot of these reviews cite the doormaker rework as being a problem. The current doormaker makes infinites harder to pull off, but that is a great thing. The old doormaker was just an annoying meat sponge with the unique mechanic basically not having any unique player interaction. The current doormaker adds an interesting interaction that forces the player to find a solution to a problem they know from the beginning of act 3: Will I have enough cards/blocks that can be exhausted? Will I have consistent enough hands that I will not need draw? Will I have cards that can be self sufficient without needing to play a bunch OR have a good amount of 0-costs? Maybe these aren't always the answers, but the point is the new doormaker offers UNIQUE problems the other bosses do not have. This makes the run way more interesting and is good design IMO. Maybe he could use a little tuning where each cycle has a door phase to give the player some breathing room/setup time or something, but the game is in a better state because of the current design.  tldr buy game and get good

[i]Slay the Spire 2's[/i] predecessor is a cornerstone of modern deckbuilding games. Having owned it on mobile it got me through countless boring lectures, meetings, and family gatherings; and its successor has always had quite a lot to live up to.  Slay the Spire 2 is all that I could have asked for and more, and has already delivered on much of what I wanted to see in a sequel.   Yes, the game is in early access, and this definitely shows in places. The difficulty curve can feel uneven, and some design elements can feel rough around the edges. But ultimately the game still feels great in spite of these minor flaws. The gameplay loop has been refined while keeping the same addictive spirit, but the new additions and choices you make feel more consequential than before. Card enchantments and new end of act boons increase player agency and help to make each run that much more unique, and I can only encourage more enchantments and ancients to be added to the game.  The expanded lore is another highlight. Uncovering the timeline and piecing together the game’s secrets adds an extra layer of engagement, especially for players who enjoy digging into worldbuilding. I’m particularly excited to dive into the bestiary once it’s available and see what new details emerge.  If you’re a fan of the first game, or deckbuilders in general, STS2 is an easy recommendation. The game isn't perfect, but at the moment that’s part of the appeal. If you want a finished product where you never have to adapt or change your strategies, I recommend waiting until the full release. But if you enjoy adapting to new challenges and watching a game evolve over time, STS2 is absolutely a must buy.  I’m excited to continue [strike]wasting my time[/strike] ascending the Spire.

Ironclad and Defect were the hardest ones, rest was relatively a smooth sail. Queen became my arch-nemesis on defect's A10, but at last I gave her a cathartic double-voltaic treatment. Overall, had lots of fun, some rage moments, zero to none bugs, plain zero crashes, while sitting in beta branch from the first beta release (yes, I was amongst the first to fall victim to the new Doormaker). So, I am not one who usually reviews games on steam. I know I tend to take this written section a bit too seriously, and I doubt many people really want to read that. However, I have heard that the current review culture for this game is a bit heavily negative for reasons I do not personally understand. So in an effort to try and make things as clear as possible, here is my take on what this game is, and the kind of players who would enjoy it.  First: Genre. Slay the Spire 2 is a true roguelite, not an "arcadelike." While there is some potential for busted builds, especially in custom runs, that is not the main point here. This is not a game where every single victory is the result of becoming massively overpowered, nor should it be balanced as such. This is not that genre of game.  Second: Difficulty. Slay the Spire 2 is NOT an easy game. I can see it potentially being a bit easier than the original game, simply due to the increased number of viable ways to play the game. But it is also not impossibly challenging. Games of this genre are designed around "learning" being the ultimate tool for growth, not some in game mechanic. If do not enjoy games that take time to learn how to play correctly, this is not the game for you. But, even as someone who struggled heavily in the original, I find this one much easier to enjoy and even improve at.  3: Randomness. This is more the fault of this genre as a whole than something that can be pinned on this game in particular, but it is something I fixate on enough myself that I feel it warrants discussion. Slay the Spire 2 is truly random in a lot of ways. The available paths, the options at the start of each act, what cards are offered, what relics are offered, what order you draw what cards in. This is not a game where the player is in control of absolutely everything, (outside of custom runs,) and if you cannot stand the feeling of "being cheated" because of RNG, this is not the right game for you. I do find it somewhat more manageable than the original game because of the more varied ways to play, but there is a heavy amount of luck involved. Especially for new players.  4: Early Access. Please keep in mind that this game is still in early access. There is a full, polished, playable game here already, with only some missing artwork and variations not yet included in regards to "base content." And yet the developers are doing something amazing, and choosing to release what could be considered a finished game as "early access" so that they can continue to improve and refine it. This, of course, includes balancing. So please keep in mind that, especially while this game is in early access, every patch they release comes with a very high likelihood of changing the balance of certain aspects of the game. Some things may become better, while other things may become worse. Your absolute favorite build may stop working entirely because of a balance patch that you personally disagree with. If this is something you can't handle, I highly recommend at least waiting until a full, 1.0 release of this game where such changes may become less likely.  Finale: Overall Recommendation. As a novice veteran of Roguelikes, Roguelites, and Card Games in general, I absolutely adore this game. My personal impression is one of absolute bewilderment that such a polished and well made game is still listed as only version 0.1x. I fully believe it is already worth the price tag, IF this is the genre of game you enjoy. But this is not a genre that is designed for everyone, and much like the Soulslike genre, not everyone is going to be able to play well enough to truly enjoy it. This is not a bad thing, and everyone is still welcome to try. But with the sheer variety of games out there, even just here on steam, your money may be worth more to you elsewhere if you do not like games that challenge you in ways you won't always be able to control or know how to get better at.

Damn people are defecating all over this game. Frankly, I love this game but I also see its problems so I'm going to try to do a fair review here. If anybody sees this genuinely wondering if this game is good, yeah it's worth 25 dollars.  The good:  -The characters feel different. Each one has their pros and cons which is great.  -The art style is awesome, the sound design is acceptable and it runs great. -Multiplayer! -There's an actual narrative to this one, which is awesome. I love the backstory, the easter eggs, seeing how character designs play into the lore, etc. No world context was my biggest complaint from StS1. -Discovering a synergy or a combo feels awesome to pull off. Cloning storm is so funny. -Many characters have different playstyles that can be blended together really effectively, like Osty Buffs and Souls, or Powers + Claw.  The bad: (Doormaker is not on this list, just don't exhaust your best cards lol) -This isn't really a strategy game. This is a "Pray and Play" game, which looks really similar but isn't. Get a big deck, pray it doesn't give you your cards in the worst order possible, and play. You could argue that following a theme like vulnerable/dominate for ironclad or poison for Silent is a strategy. I would counter that by saying that infants use strategy to identify shapes like circles or squares. Anybody can associate concepts. -You're actively discouraged for removing cards in your deck, to an unreasonable degree. If you have 18 cards, removing 1 increases the likelihood of seeing all the other, better ones. However, if you buy 2 cards, you automatically get 2 cards that are better than the one you'd remove anyway and statistically it's roughly the same. And you can't keep removing cards, since the price to remove goes up every time. Taken to scale, there's no reason to carefully consider what you do and do not want when you should just be filling your deck. This doesn't feel BAD exactly, since you'll probably hybrid 2 different playstyles anyway, but it is really boring. Why incentivize not thinking in a strategy game? This doesn't even include multiplayer, where my friends keep putting cards into my deck or having me draw ethereal cards (disappears for the combat if you don't play them) (echo form). - There's no way of predicting which of the 7 ancients you're going to get, and there's no way of influencing the odds. They offer radically different boons for characters and "strategizing" around the hope of seeing A) the right one B) with the right item is just a worthless and frankly stupid thing to do. I haven't see the soot head for 80 hours. -Some of the MOST effective builds revolve around you just not playing the game. You can juggle orbs, anger, pommel strike, Sly cards, colorless cards (with regent, but very hard), and right hand hand. This is because, when there's no strategy, you should eliminate all RNG. - This game is still early access, so this could change, but some fights just feel oppressive and boring. The Decamillipede comes to mind, where it's just 3 segments non-stop attacking you. Why does the middle attack twice? And how?  My fixes? - Introduce a sidebar! It would be cool to be able to store some cards between runs, acts, or even floors after combat. Just a "Hey I'll take this in case I get more of these cards, but I'll remove it now since it sucks on its own" or maybe "Hey Hunter Killer could be next maybe I should bring sword boomerang or Bludgeon" to, you know, strategize? - Some sort of sacrifice system to play the odds. At any time, you can burn your sidebar cards to influence your odds for a specific ancient, or maybe you could pay gold/cards to get a specific relic you want? Some sort of risk/reward to... strategize around? - Get away from StS1! You already made that game. Lean into what is REALLY good and unique about this game. Card enchantments, quests, and incorporating lore bits (Have characters drop lines if they play specific cards in a certain order, especially if it's a GOOD order, to reward the players who play the game "correctly").  It's fun! But eventually you aren't slaying the spire, you're "touring" the spire on autopilot. Slay the Spire had this problem too, which is why I thought they made a 2nd one, but now I don't know.

If you enjoyed Slay the Spire 1, you will likely enjoy Slay the Spire 2.  If you haven't played Slay the Spire, this game is still approachable, and while my review is written from the perspective of someone who has a couple hundred hours on the first game on another platform, I still know multiple people who started with this one and seem to enjoy it. Just know that 1) this is a roguelite deckbuilder (winning one run is not the end) and 2) this game is in early access so some art is unfinished and mechanics are regularly being adjusted based on in-game feedback from players.  Anyways, I'm excited to see the direction Mega Crit goes with the new mechanics introduced such as alternate acts, enemies that can 'afflict' your cards, and card enchantments. While I think the new 'quest' card types could be more interesting than the current 'fancy curses' that they basically are at the moment, the idea still has a lot of potential too. The rework of boss relics into 'ancient relics' that you pick while seeing the next act's map is an especially great adjustment, and the relics often feel a lot more interesting and influential on my runs.  I also appreciate the adjustments to pre-existing game features; there's a lot of great QoL stuff. There being 10 ascensions instead of 20 is also a good change (20 categories of difficulty is overwhelming in a system where you can only climb difficulties one at a time per character), although I will warn that the difficulty jump from ascension 8 to 9 is probably more intense than any difficulty jumps in StS1. I also miss certain StS1 ascensions such 'deadlier events'. I also like how the unlocks, instead of just being tied to 'how many points you have', are now tied to 'epochs' in a lore timeline (even though in many ways it is still the same points unlock system)-- even in games without a story focus, I think just a little bit of info on character backstories + motivations goes a long way.  Speaking of characters-- I think both new characters are very fun. Regent's my personal favorite, although Necrobinder is probably the better-made character. The returning characters all have had their own adjustments as well, and while I think Ironclad does have some room for improvement, the new discard mechanics for Silent and *especially* the new status-focused cards for Defect are awesome. While Watcher isn't in this game as of now, some of her strategies live on in spirit through the new characters and some of her cards/abilities are actually still there as colorless cards or boss relics. Rushdown is not one of these cards.  Multiplayer is also MUCH BETTER than I expected it would be. It's different from the board game-- everyone is in the same fight at the same time and there's no way to buy things for each other in shops-- but it is still enjoyable and feels balanced at all player counts. The multiplayer-exclusive cards are also a cool addition, and I hope that additional updates might add multiplayer-exclusive relics, events, or custom mode variants (custom mode doesn't have a lot currently but it was never really a focus of the first game so that's reasonable).  Finally, I want to highlight the graphics + audio. The animations make the enemies and player characters feel so much more *alive* in comparison to the first game, and the soundtrack is much more adaptive in ways that enhance boss fights. The artwork for cards is cool with powerful relic-based cards having 'full art' and multiplayer cards featuring cute interactions between the characters-- plus, as this is early access, we get to see beta/placeholder art in its natural environment in all its MS paint glory.  Overall, this is a fantastic game and I highly recommend playing it (or waiting for full release if you don't want to do early access).

Let's start with the basics: Is the game fun?   Short answer: absolutely, I can't stop playing it!   Longer answer: The way that Slay the spire 2 plays and it's core gameplay loop is perfect for replay-ability, the mechanics are fun and it feels like the game is already full of fun events, cards, enemies, characters, etc. So there is already plenty of content for an early access game. The difficulty ramps steadily up and it does get pretty hard sometimes, but not in a way that it feels unfair. You get rewarded for playing your cards right!   Is the game polished?  I haven't encountered any bugs or glitches, I've seen some "exploits" online but it feels like you have to go and actively search for those. The game runs easily and the engine they've used works well. Game just feels polished. And also even though the game is in early access there is a multiplayer mode which the first game didn't even have. Most early access games would add multiplayer in a content update.   Devs and early access  Mega Crit regularly updates the game and they communicate frequently to their community. The recent review bombing seems completely unfair and this game should definitely not be sitting at a mixed review rating. It seems a certain part of the community really enjoys being able to play in a certain way (infinites) and ofcourse the infinites are very fun and dopamine inducing so I get that but the developers felt they were to easy to achieve. They communicated that and nerfed accordingly. I can only respect that, it's still able to achieve but just harder. The developers also have a monthly newsletter where they share updates, future plans and interact with the community. Very cool!  Is it worth the price?  I personally think even though it already has a lot of content, it could still be a couple euros less as it's now around 23 euros. I would say 18 euros would be a better price point. But when the game is completely developed the 23 euros could for sure be a good price.    STS2 is surprisingly polished and there is already much to do, much to discover and lots of potential for replay-ability. The thrill of building a deck that works feels very good and makes you feel like you've actually earned your win, simply said it makes you feel very overpowered. On the other hand the game is also hard and can be very punishing, but let's be fair. Why play a roguelike deckbuilder where every run IS a win? Shouldn't you have to feel like you played your cards well and played good? This game delivers on that very well. It's also very cool that the developers update the game regularly in a "beta-branch" this makes it seem they listen to community feedback and they've already shown that they indeed do listen.   Slay The Spire 2 is an amazingly fun deckbuilding game and you should play it.

Before anything, I don’t usually write reviews, but I felt really compelled to do so for this game.  I’m honestly baffled by how many negative reviews there are, because this is an AMAZING game. Even setting aside the underdog backstory (which is worth looking into), the game delivers in almost every way imaginable.  TL;DR: You should buy this game if you have any interest in deck-building games, want something simple and fun you can play in short bursts, or, if you’re like me, enjoy doing math in a video game.  Cons: - Some battles can be downright miserable if you don’t know they’re coming. If you’ve played before, you already know the three monsters I’m talking about. BUT if you do know about them and build accordingly, you’ll be surprised how manageable they become. - Multiplayer could use more unique mechanics. Team buff cards are cool, but I’d love to see more depth. Like attacks that target specific players vs. the whole team, a formation system (frontline taking more hits), or even setup turns where you know you’re safe. That kind of design would really encourage more strategic deck building. - You have to be okay with losing. Real talk, you’re going to lose a lot. Accept it. That said, once you build a strong deck, you can absolutely breeze through runs.  Pros: - The satisfaction of building a strong deck is unmatched. You feel uniquely powerful based on whatever combo you create. You don’t even need an infinite—just stumbling into a clever, strong synergy feels amazing and makes you feel like the monsters should be afraid of you. - Multiplayer is fantastic and long overdue. My friends and I loved the first game, but talking about it always felt like “you had to be there.” Now you can actually experience those moments together—watching a friend go infinite on a boss, and even contributing to it with cooperative cards. That’s where the game really shines. - The graphics are a step up from the first game and look great. Even the “proxy” art feels intentional in a good way. I didn’t even realize it was placeholder art until someone pointed it out. - It’s simple and easy to jump into, even if you only have a few minutes. - The new characters add a much-needed layer of variety. My favorite is Necrobinder—her mechanics are really interesting and fun to play with. Based on what I’ve seen, I’d love to see more characters added in future updates. Honestly, I’d even pay for them as DLC, which I almost never say. The game feels that well made.  All of that is to say: I genuinely think you’ll enjoy this game a lot. Don’t let the negative reviews sway you—give it a shot yourself.  Especially if you’ve got a friend to climb the tower with.

For STS1 I think I waited until about 500 hours to leave my review.  This time I'm doing it shy of 300 because I want to push back against negative reviewers.  Slay the Spire is a game developed by a deckbuilding game nerd.  The guy who does most of the design used to run a fan-site for Android Netrunner for chrisssake!  What that means is that the central tenet that informs everything about the game is the idea that every strategy should be viable and yet none should be sufficient.    Both of these design principles have the effect of increasing run variation and making each individual decision more interesting and difficult.  After all, if there exists a proscribed strategy that is easily scrutable and always wins, that renders the game no longer interesting.  Instead, one has to try to eke out some tiny advantage from every choice to make it across the finish line.  This is all a very long-winded way of saying that, out of every gaming experience I've ever had, Slay the Spire does the best job of making every single decision in the game both interesting and impactful.  This is an impressive feat.  And to fans upsetty spaghetti that their pet card or strategy has been changed to no longer be the brainless best choice in every scenario I say, "You don't understand why this game is good in the first place."

Looking at my playtime one might think that I'm somewhat decent at the game and that my opinion is well formed and relevant. That couldn't be further from truth. A look at other reviewers' playtime will give you a hint. No matter how you feel about it this is a game that takes an incredibly long time to get and even longer to master. In that sense it is incredibly satisfying to play and seeing your progress. That being said it isn't a game without flaw and here's breakdown of what one may consider good or bad about it.  ========== The Bad ========== I start with the bad because I feel that a lot of the western community might be trying to avoid mentioning due to the current state of reviews and review bombing.  - Slay the Spire 2, much like its predecessor is a game you either spend tens of hours playing or are better off refunding. The commitment is real and if you want to see all that this game has to offer you have to play at least a few tens of runs each lasting a really bare minimum of half an hour. Thankfully you don't have to do any of that in one sitting but if you don't feel like wasting days of your life playing a single a game that's reasonable,  - Card design is not always intuitive. This is something that might be fixed as the early access progresses but there is a point to be made that cards that do the same thing are sometimes worded differently and the interactions between them are not always easy to tell without some trial and error. This is not something that comes up constantly and once you experience a run or two with all characters it will no longer matter but it is still a hurdle that might trouble a beginner. - The art style is not for everyone. While personally I adore the cartoon-y not very serious aesthetic this game goes for I have had a few friends tell me that it really doesn't sit right with them, even when showcasing the game to them live. You can mostly tell if you like the aesthetics from the steam preview but I feel like it still is worth a mention. I should point out that a friend even mentioned that they could not tell relics (a form passive beneficial item in game) from potions (one use benefits) apart because their designs are sometimes too similar. - Game balance is still not necessarily perfect in early access. I personally play on the public beta branch which is a few updates ahead of the main branch and I can say that there is a definite feels-bad moment when a new balance patch comes out and it turns out that the strategy I had just gotten comfortable with was nerfed or completely removed because the developer saw run statistics and understood it to be too powerful. That being said, it is sensible for a game that wants to be challenging to nerf good strategies forcing players to explore others more deeply. It's just that, for now, until early access is over there is a somewhat tiresome (but necessary) cycle of discovering how to play the game correctly and then having that ruined with the next update. - Dark patterns. While I usually don't like the use of this term because I feel like it makes it sound like these "patterns" are some form of intentional malicious act from the developers, it is true that this game has some of them. The biggest being the element of chance which is ever-present in almost all stages of the game. That being said those patterns, while addictive are not exploited explicitly to make the player spend more time with the game. It seems quite clear that the developers with all their design decisions, communication with players etc. just want to make the game enjoyable and interesting rather than addictive.  ========== The Good ========== - This is possibly the first game that I've seen and think makes good use of early access. It has a somewhat clear outline of what it wants to do within its context (balance out all characters by observing actual play data, fix bugs that might have otherwise required day one hotfixes etc) while also having a release date promise that seems plausible (allegedly summer 2027, but the devs don't want to commit to that statement). - It is incredibly fun (yes this comes after good use of early access because I actually find that more impressive). It's only been a few weeks since the release but I've already committed hundreds of hours to exploring the incredible depths of decision making that this games allows you to go into, This shows to me that - The existence of multiplayer along with the ability to draw on the map is a genuinely unexpected blessing this game has brought us. I am not exaggerating in that while playing this game with friends I've spent more time drawing faces, memes and other stupid things on them map than actually worrying about the real game. In a way it's as if the devs unintentionally left a small version of skribbl io in their game as a bonus thing to spend time one with friends. It is fun, it is dumb and it is genuinely something I didn't expect would affect my experience with the game as much as it did. - It encourages expanding your skills outside the game to get better at it. While this might sound like a bit of a stretch I've seen various players (myself included) try to build tools with programming languages or simple statistical tools (like excel) to evaluate their performance in the game, the effect some of their choices have on their runs etc. While it is obviously not necessary for a player to bust out a set of complicated scripts and statistical parsers to actually become good at it, it seems that there is an incentive here moreso than other games as I've seen lots of people doing it. - The previous point also leads me to mentioning the incredible modding support provided almost by default since the developers moved to Godot as a game engine. Mods are always a very nice way to introduce prospective game developers to the kind of work they have to do without having them take on the challenge of building a full game from scratch and thankfully this game also allows for that to happen without it feeling unfair or immersion breaking. Mods that add new characters, cards, relics or other things are almost always a delight to see (even if I don't usually play with them) as they show the community's creative side and love for the game. More practical mods (such as integrated stats measuring mods) are also there to aid that deeper understanding of the game that I've mentioned a million times already.  All in all, I'm sure I've missed a lot of things worth mentioning (for example I specifically made no mention about the music which I find just ok) but the overall takeaway is that Slay the Spire 2 is an incredibly time consuming but equally rewarding game in its complexity and difficulty. It is not necessarily for everyone but it is definitely worth its money if you're into genre or if you think you might be interested.  As for the early access, I know a lot of people have a policy against buying games like that but if there is one early access game to buy I think this would be the one. It is already in a state where it could sell as a full game and if it did no-one would complain. the only reason you should not buy it right now is if you don't want to be part of the dev teams balance metrics for patching, which is valid but not something that most will care about.

# For Ascensions < 8  Edit: I only play on Ascension 10 but after replaying the game all the way from Ascension 0 again, the game feels very easy. Able to easily climb with perfect win streak. Pro players can do the same on Ascension >= 8. For my experience as a casual on Ascension >= 8 see below. TL;DR it feels a bit hard but that's what I also enjoy about the game, sometimes a run becomes way too easy which becomes unfun.  # For Ascensions >= 8  Runs don't work if you're unable to find any decent block e.g. Unmovable, Stone Armor on Ironclad or Footwork on Silent or probably Fasten or one of the enchants given by Pael. Regent and Defect are ok with decent passive block, you still need to find frost orbs or Pillars of Creation but their block card stats are higher anyway.  If you don't get these, you need to have ungodly amounts of draw and just go infinite on turn 1, which is also not reliable since you don't guarantee the cards you draw on turn 1. Sometimes it works on Ironclad and Silent but you won't have HP left until you get to the boss. Something needs to be done to give you at least one of these 2 options. I know you're not supposed to win every run but having a run where you just can't build a deck because the options aren't given to you doesn't feel good.  That being said in runs in which you do see them or just find something broken like Corruption, Runic Pyramid, Apparition, the run gets absolutely broken quickly and it's barely fun from that point on because I already I know I won in Act 1/2.  So would value if there's something that still keeps the game engaging but also gives you enough option so that runs don't end up in a loss without a fault of your own of not having the game giving you block or turn 1 wins.  Nonetheless, enjoyable game. Could also use more replay-ability - hopefully keep adding new characters :)  Also bring something like Dark Embrace/Corruption/Second Wind. Playing those to win on turn 1 is so satisfying! Drop the rarity for those cards and make the game harder for fun runs too?!

Let me make this clear, Slay the Spire 2 is a rouge-like, dungeon crawler, deckbuilding game. So it's supposed to be hard. That being said, it's a bit TOO hard. I will talk about my solo experiences and co-op experiences.  TL;DR: The balancing and scaling is just broken. Might be a skill issue idk.  Solo: The game is quite fun actually! I love the first Slay the Spire and it feels somewhat balanced. Then I heard about this game, and I got quite excited because of the co-op feature. I thought it would be like the board game where you can play solo or with friends. Now for my solo experience, it felt fine at first, but sometimes it feels like I have to gamble what cards I keep, or how many depending on the later act bosses. I tend to do fine for the first and second act, but once I get to the third? All hell breaks loose. Unfathomably unbalanced enemies, ridiculously hard bosses like the Doormaker and Test Subject, or just plain dumb gimmicks for what is supposed to be a "regular enemy". Even the other bosses should be reworked like The Insatiable, Kaiser Crab, Knowledge Demon, and Vantom. Fun game, but terrible balancing.  Co-op: This is where the game starts to fall off hard. Me and a few friends play the game thinking everything will go smoothly. But no, the biggest issue I can see as of now is the fact that the scaling is complete and utter trash. The HP for the enemies would essentially be multiplied by each player. Meaning a normal enemy at 30 HP with 3 players would be like 90 HP. Which would be fine if so many enemies didn't stack strength like there's no tomorrow or if the player health scales along with the amount of players. I feel like the best way to balance it is to add 50% base health to the enemies for each player instead of 100%. Normal enemies aren't even the worst part about this issue, it's the Elite and boss enemies. That on top of the silly gimmicks that each one has. My buddies and I really try to focus on which cards to play first but then we end up with like 4 status cards and a single block or strike card. That's also another thing that I have noticed, is it just me or do common and status cards get cycled in your hand more often than uncommon or rare cards? It just makes the game unbearable and frustrating instead of fun and strategic.  In conclusion, I understand this game is in "Early Access" and I hate to add onto this "review bombing" and I know that there is a function to give feedback but I genuinely do believe that the devs are trying to fix things that aren't inherently broken like the rework to the Doormaker as an example. I truly hope this game does get balanced and some enemies and systems get reworked, otherwise I will keep this negative review until these issues get dealt with. I may not be the most experienced player in the world but I would like the game to be enjoyable, not easier or harder. Just less frustrating.
