Slay the Spire 2 builds on the success of the first game adding new classes and cards. If you enjoyed the first game or want to try a deck builder, STS and STS2 remain the premier games in the genre.  There are several subtle improvements over the first game, but not enough to completely make the first game obsolete. At the same time, there is also no reason not to jump straight into STS2.  I have a few criticisms about game balance and design, but If you are new to the game or are not looking to push to the highest difficulty on every character, you can pretty much ignore any discourse about balance or the sentiment held by some that the game is too easy, the game is great, go play.   It is also worth saying that the game is being patched fairly regularly so many of the criticisms around balance are subject to change, but here are a few thoughts then about the current state of balance in STS2 as of writing this review.  1) Many of the mechanics of the elites and bosses feel flat. The issue is that many of the fights feel like a block or damage check rather than having meaningful card interactions as solutions to overcoming their mechanics. A good example of great design is Phrog Parasite, not only do you need to think about drafting cards as a solution to his split phase, but you also need to decide which turn you want to pop him on, it combines drafting and strategic play in a very satisfying way.  2) After beating Act 2, the run often feels over. If you have been able to beat the Act 2 bosses, it typically means that your deck is already scaling well and Act 3 will not pose much of a threat, the turns start to play themselves (shout out to Vakuu).

The predecessor of this game didn't establish the genre, but it set the bar all others in it strive to reach. The difficulty, mechanical density, and satisfaction of The Loop was as close to perfect as any deck building roguelike game has ever managed to come.  Until the sequel. Somehow, Mega Crit has done it again. This isn't too surprising given that they basically just took the winning formula of Slay the Spire 1 and added layers of improvement--new cards, new characters, new events, and most importantly in my opinion, the multiplayer game mode. Solo, or with friends, you will lose hours to this game. The runs are just long enough to get you invested without being so involved that you feel too frustrated by a late loss that you don't want to take another swing at it.  A big way I feel like this game has improved is in the variety of deck building options the game not only offers, but demands of you as you rise up in Ascension level. Even a middling player can get away with basically any silly or sub-optimal build at low Ascension, which is great for people learning the game and experimenting with all the various cards and synergies. Early complaints mentioned that the game pushed certain "high level infinite combos" at the cost of build variety in order to win, and while those are obviously extremely powerful when you can pull them off, they are by no means necessary to pull a win at even the highest difficulty level. Every deck archetype has bad match-ups that can be run ending at that level of play--success comes not from getting lucky enough to avoid them, but from knowing they're out there and adding a couple contingencies to your deck to deal with those worse case scenarios.  All in all, if you loved the first Spire, you'll love the second one even more. If this is your introduction to the series, you couldn't hope to find a better one.   On a side note, review bombing comes from a time-honored tradition of protesting developers engaging in shady/unethical business practices. Using it to try and bully developers into not making tweaks and adjustments to a game still in its testing phase only hurts the game you clearly care so much about. There are appropriate channels IN GAME to leave feedback and the developers have proven that they take that feedback seriously. They are using those channels and data collected from player gameplay to make their balance decisions, instead of making them on the short-sighted whims of people still riding the power trip of setting Arrowhead on fire. I admire the spirit of collective action, but it is being sorely misapplied here.

RNG can be frustrating sometimes when trying to get a card to tie an OP build together, which can ruin a run, but it happens. My advice when playing that will help. Always pay the gold to get rid of extra cards at merchants (non playable first, then standard strike and defend cards), always plan your route to hit as many rest sites as possible, take offensive AOE cards early and when you get the opportunity to take a greed card for big gold at start, always take it. Sometimes you get unlucky and have no blocking cards when every enemy is attacking you, but that's just how rogue-likes are. Every now and then you end up biting the bullet and it's super frustrating, and then every now and then you manage to play your cards just right and actually make it to the end. That feeling of accomplishment makes the gameplay worth it all. Whenever the half-baked build you have starts popping off leads to some awesome levels of fun. I genuinely think that the people review bombing the game are probably impatient players, and also don't know how to read the cards.  One of the best ways to play this game is definitely with a friend or two. Any of the struggles you face as you climb the tower feel far more manageable with more people by your side. I'd even say the game is just plain better with the multiplayer, definitely tons of fun. Also, being able to draw on the map now is super funny, especially if you have some buddies with you.  Summary: 10/10 game, does not deserve the review bombing going on right now, people probably just can't read the cards and plan ahead. I guess rogue-likes/-lites aren't for everyone, but if you generally enjoy that genre I highly recommend giving this a try.

A strong start to the second entry of the STS franchise (crazy to say that).  Really loving the game, and a lot of thought and care has clearly gone into it.  I still think there are growing pains to get through, but i'm excited to see where it goes.   My main complaint is the questions the act3 bosses ask of the player arent as interesting as the STS1 bosses. Queen asks you to draw cards (which your deck should already be doing), and door maker still feels like a mess. Test subject is easily my favorite because it asks you to have nonlinear scaling/kill him fast twice.  overall, still greatly enjoying it. The game still needs some work, but already I think Slay the Spire II is on track to be a significantly better game than its predecessor.  I'm liking a lot of the new enemies: a lot of them have really annoying gimmicks that encourage you to have a multifaceted deck of cards instead of just brute forcing everything with an inventory of 300 damage swords.  ...it doesn't really stop me, but I appreciate the effort.  For all the grumbling in these reviews about difficulty, I think that Slay the Spire 2 is honestly way too easy.  It took me weeks to clear the first boss of the original game, and meanwhile with the sequel I made it to the third boss on my first playthrough ever and A10'd in about two weeks. But by the time I reach the end of Act III, I feel like my journey up the Spire is only just beginning: concepts of a plan are forming, as slowly ideas for how to make this build work are formulating in my head.  And then it's over. And I'm kind of just sit there feeling blue-balled. I don't know. Maybe a bunch of players have made "really good at Slay the Spire" part of their identity and found themselves really frustrated when they couldn't immediately win runs... but that's a good thing: no one wants a roguelike you can exhaust of challenges in two weeks.  I'm not super fond of how the somber and forlorn feeling of the original game has kind of been given Terminator 2 treatment and replaced with something wacky and whimsical. It's probably the objectively correct decision for what this game's trying to be, but I do think the moodiness was a distinctive quality of the original. After all: me, my 300 damage sword, and my bag of eighty five relics that have long escaped the confines of the game window would probably feel like a remarkable tonal clash with the grey atmosphere of the original game. (oh man, limited relic slots would be a great ascension)  Even so, it's already clearly the better game. While build metas do exist, the fact that the game doesn't entirely revolve around forming hyperspecific decks makes it a lot more strategically engaging than its predecessor, where you would just spam "shivdeck" for twenty consecutive ascensions and then go install another game.

I don’t usually leave reviews, but I feel like I need to help drown out the negativity from people who don’t really understand the game they’re buying. It seems like a lot of players either aren’t coming from StS1 or don’t understand how the devs handle early access. Unlike many other EA games, MegaCrit is deeply involved in actually using early access to shape the game, and it’s ironic that the reviews end up punishing them for it. StS1 was balanced to a T because of its long early access period.  There are also people who don’t understand how roguelikes work. You aren’t meant to win every run. If you don’t have fun unless you win, then this genre just isn’t for you.  And A10 is supposed to be hard. You aren’t meant to win every A10 unless you’re really, really good. In fact, the current A10 in StS2 is easier than StS’s A20. There’s a high skill ceiling that isn’t immediately apparent to people who aren’t playing at a high level. Watch a high-level player before saying A10 is too hard. Or just play on lower Ascensions if you need to win to have fun.  One thing I will say from all this discourse is that StS 1/2 could do a better job communicating the purpose of its difficulty levels. Maybe a different structure that doesn’t frame A10 as the “endgame” everyone should be playing on. I’m not sure. As it stands, people’s egos seem to get in the way of choosing a lower, more enjoyable difficulty for themselves.  I trust MegaCrit will stay true to their design and not be swayed by these reviews. I have a lot of respect for this series and the intention and care behind it's design.

Slay the Spire 2 is already in a pretty good spot, especially for how early it is in early access. The core gameplay is exactly what made the first game so strong. It feels familiar in the right ways without feeling stale, and it’s clear the foundation is solid and that the developers know what they’re doing.  That said, it’s not finished yet, which should be obvious given both the early access label and the developers’ stated intent. Despite that there’s already enough here to support interesting runs and experimentation with different strategies for hundreds of hours.  A lot of the complaints seem to come from a disconnect in expectations around difficulty, particularly with Ascension 10, which is currently the highest level. Ascensions are completely optional and are designed to make the game more challenging for players who actively want that experience. If Ascension 10 feels punishing, that’s largely the point. The base game remains very playable without engaging with those higher, optional difficulty modifiers.  Some criticism around RNG and difficulty at lower Ascension levels tends to reflect a lack of familiarity with the game’s systems rather than a fundamental design issue. The game rewards experience, pattern recognition, and decision-making over time, and part of its appeal is the learning curve as players improve and refine their approach.  The recent wave of negative reviews from the Chinese player base is due to balance changes that reduced or removed easily exploitable infinite strategies. Adjustments are good for the long-term health and balance of the game. For players who prefer a less constrained experience, modding already provides ways to customize cards, mechanics, or difficulty to suit individual preferences.  Overall, most of the criticism seems to come down to expectations rather than any real issues with the core design. As it stands, the game already has a strong foundation, and with continued development, it has a good chance of surpassing the first in nearly every way.

Review bombing a game just because its hard shouldnt be the way things are done. It's called RNG, all actions taken are your own responsibility to try and make work.  Sure i probably cannot speak for everyone as I am only at 72 hours, and god knows how much from STS 1 on this and other forms, but I know going in that unless i get lucky and get the cards i want for a specific build, it is NOT going to work.   Am i going to get mad because I never saw the cards I needed? No, because that is how RNG worked this game. So I start a new run until the build i want, happens. I rarely leave reviews, but I cannot stand by and have people spam: "Only certain builds can win" - False, I have played around multiple times and gotten out some wins, some builds are not meant for elites. "X or Y is a trash character" - False, each character has different playstyles, and you can build them in any way you want and still get a win. (Again, RNG comes into play) It depends on how much are you willing to risk to get that win. "Floor monsters are harder than elites / or elites are harder than some bosses" - Debatable, I say this because how you build your deck decides how fights end up, and of course your first few turns. So while there is some balancing that could be done here and there, It is how the game goes. Again.... this is based on how you start building out your deck, if you pick X because you want to do something stupid later on and don't want to miss out, then you have to bear the consequences of that card you bloated your deck with.  I guarantee a lot of the people complaining probably get more than 30 cards in their deck with barely any draw cards and cry about it.  That's my 2 cents, I support this Dev, I like the direction it is going. If I wanted an easier game to play and turn off my brain, I would go play something else. This dev doesn't need to keep adjusting their balance changes because you want to cry about it.   This is their vision - let them create it.
